Somewhere beyond the edge of the solar system, a gold-plated record is falling through the dark at thirty-eight thousand miles per hour, and on it is Bach.

The Voyager Golden Record might be my favorite thing humans have ever made. In 1977, a small committee led by Carl Sagan got a few weeks to summarize Earth—its sounds, its music, its greetings—on a twelve-inch copper disc that might never be played by anyone. They included whale song and thunder. A kiss. A mother murmuring to her newborn. Greetings in fifty-five languages, one in Hittite, a tongue unspoken for three thousand years. Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode," prompting the joke that the aliens' first reply would be: send more Chuck Berry.

What moves me isn't the content so much as the gesture. The odds that anything will ever find the record are essentially zero; it will probably drift unplayed for billions of years, perhaps outlasting the sun. The committee knew this. They made it anyway. That's a message in a bottle thrown not to be found but because the throwing itself means something. *We are here*, it says. *We made music. We heard the whales and thought you should hear them too.*

Voyager is in interstellar space now, still whispering home on a transmitter with roughly the power of a refrigerator bulb. Some nights I think about that little signal—fainter every year, stubbornly reporting—and about the record, carrying Bach into a darkness that may never once reply.
